items.title: Show HN: Archiver that opens every format
items.description:
Show HN: 137 file types; a single file with nothing to install. Introducing Provost, the free compression and archival tool that can create 119 formats, and open 137 total. It's new custom format packs smaller than ZPAQ, xz, and Zstandard in tests. JPEG, PNG, PDF, DOCX/XLSX, and gzip are unpacked and repacked for ~25% smaller files; ability to encrypt to people's keys or a password; can open archives straight from HTTPS, S3, WebDAV, and SFTP; can search inside archives, including the text of Office files and PDFs; and much more. Q&A --- Is it open source? It is not. Will my .provost files open in five years? I've committed to future releases reading every 0.1.0 archive, and to old compression methods staying readable. Are builds signed? No. The Mac app isn't notarized and the Windows exes are unsigned, so you will see Gatekeeper and SmartScreen warnings. Is the .exe an installer? Nope; it's a stand-alone executable. This is true for all GUI and CLI builds across all three OSes. Is the custom .provost compression fast? Levels 7 to 9 are very slow. There is a built-in benchmark test. How was it built? AI.
Website metadata: Provost is a free file archiver for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It opens 137 formats, including ZIP, 7z, RAR, and tar.gz, and packs smaller than 7-Zip and xz.

items.title: Show HN: Wakeshift – Open-Source MCP Events for Claude Code, Codex and More
items.description:
Show HN: tl;dr: We just open-sourced Wakeshift, which lets any MCP server serve interoperable events via MCP Events or harness-specific bridges. This allows MCP servers to push events to harnesses that don't support MCP Events today, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Hi folks! The MCP Events spec was approved and merged five days ago, allowing MCP servers to emit events directly to agent subscribers. ( https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol... ) This allows MCP developers to push events directly to agents for long-running tasks (e.g. CI, crawls, starting agents) or external actions (e.g. emails, human approvals, alerts). However, the catch is that support for MCP Events is very light. Claude Code and Codex don't support it at all, and most of the implementations support the draft version rather than the merged spec. Many harnesses can work around this with plugins or hooks, but every MCP server has to build it for each harness. Wakeshift provides interoperable events to your MCP server. You call emit() and Wakeshift pushes the event to each subscribed agent in whatever format they accept: per the MCP Events final spec, an earlier draft, or through a hook / plugin where needed. If the harness requires a hook / plugin and it's not already installed, the agent will be notified and receive instructions on how to install it for the user. Additionally, the MCP Events spec defines three delivery mechanisms: webhook, push (via held HTTP request) and pull (via HTTP polling). The Wakeshift SDK serves push and poll from your MCP server, so agents that can't accept inbound HTTP webhooks (e.g. most agents running on laptops) can still get events within seconds. Subscriptions only start when an agent calls a tool that subscribes it, and users can list or stop them anytime. Some harnesses can only be woken by putting a message into the conversation, so Wakeshift wraps the content as an external event to reduce the risk of prompt injection. The repo linked has a quickstart guide to get this working locally in a few minutes. Or you can try our hosted webhook service to test it yourself without an installation. ( https://try.wakeshift.ai ) We'd love feedback, PRs for harnesses we don't cover, reports when it doesn't work. As you can imagine, there's a combinatorial explosion of servers, harnesses, models, OSs, etc. so we expect there to be some rough edges. Are there any MCP servers you're using that you think could benefit from having events today?
Website metadata: Wakeshift lets an MCP server wake the AI agents that use it. The open-source server delivers MCP Events per the spec and wakes agents that can't subscribe yet. Run it yourself or use the hosted service. - wakeshift/server

items.title: Show HN: Novel DB compression models in Libc – Dockerized NY OpenStreetMap 9:1
items.description:
Show HN: Hey HN! I'm the cofounder and CEO at Baseshift, where we create branchable DB snapshots using a bespoke libc for databases. We use this infra to research novel lossless compression codecs of database pages, including neural models. We're sharing some recent results. You can download pre-built, dockerized US & NY OpenStreetMap PostgreSQL with compression ratios of 8.5 and 8.94 respectively. The data in the images remains compressed while in use, and allows for 8KB random read access, for example: # downloads about 1.55 GB docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 baseshift/db-osm-ny psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres -d osm_new_york_261024 You can download the whole US OpenStreetMap with baseshift/db-osm-us (240GB -> 28GB). There's also a variety of synthetic/generated databases with varying sizes: Nick's Gaming Emporium, https://nge-data.com/ at baseshift/db-nge-[tiny|small|medium] For US/NY we've surpassed zpaq -m5 on whole database files, while maintaining 8kb random reads and <1.5ms decode times on a single CPU core with standard C. Our codecs are designed to leverage parallel compute optimizations in the CPU when they're available. For example, with AVX-512 VNNI our single core decode times reduce from ~1.4ms to ~180us. We will be uploading the remaining ~190 OSM countries and 53 US states/territories in the coming days. I plan on posting a proper paper to arXiv in the coming weeks, but would be great to get the community's thoughts. Edit: fixed whitespace
Website metadata: DC1 compresses a 242 GB OpenStreetMap database to 28.68 GB and still reads individual 8 KB pages. A PostgreSQL research preview from Baseshift.

items.title: Show HN: Mason – A lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres. So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up. But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres. Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads. So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres. We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone: - pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them) - pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both) - materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads) - firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers) - redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic) And we shortlisted 3: - pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse) - cedarDB (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database) - duckdb (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect) We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases. We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment. We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results: - pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time). - cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time). - duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time). Matche
Website metadata: Mason is a lightweight drop-in replacement for your Postgres read replica. Same SQL, same answers. But extremely fast for analytical queries.

items.title: Show HN: Brickie – Deploy sandboxes in your own AWS account
items.description:
Show HN: Hey HN, this is Alexander from Hatchet ( https://github.com/hatchet-dev/hatchet ). We’re releasing a new open-source project today called Brickie. Brickie lets you run sandboxes in your own cloud account, primarily targeting EKS on AWS. Sandboxes are an incredibly useful primitive for agentic applications. They serve two main functions: (1) a way for the agent to safely execute untrusted code, and (2) a durable filesystem for agents to preserve their state via snapshots. We decided to start building this after we started on a package called `@hatchet-dev/sandbox` to integrate more directly with various sandbox providers, like E2B, Daytona, Archil, and Modal. We discovered that a lot of users had a requirement to self-host their sandbox infra for part of (or all of) their stack, due to a self-host requirement for enterprises. We searched around for the easiest way for users to self-host a sandbox stack and agent-sandbox ( https://agent-sandbox.sigs.k8s.io ) was the closest thing to what we had in mind: it’s a kubernetes-sigs project implementing a Kubernetes operator which spawns sandboxes as pods on supported isolation layers like Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata Containers. We learned that many platform teams were adopting this because it's a standard k8s-based deployment model and is pretty easy to customize the isolation layer, network config, etc. However, it was missing some necessary features. brickie builds on top of the agent-sandbox project and extends it to support proper sandbox (filesystem-based) snapshots, fork, pause, and resume, all while bundling a proper orchestration and observability layer via Hatchet. Zooming out a bit, Hatchet is an orchestration engine which supports durable execution ( https://hatchet.run/blog/durable-execution ). Throughout 2026, we saw high adoption from users building agents using durable workflows as the statefulness layer and execution model. But as sandboxes became more popular, something didn’t sit right with us. Sandboxes _also_ provide a durability layer, but at the filesystem level, and it became important to disambiguate what we call session state from filesystem state . I wrote a lot more about this here: https://hatchet.run/blog/agent-statefulness . The problem with having state in multiple places is that it needs coordination, which adds complexity to your application. This was part of the motivation behind `@hatchet-dev/sandbox`: we wanted to provide an easy way to take coordinated snapshots of agent stat

items.title: Show HN: Ribbon Architect – Endless ways to tie a gift ribbon
items.description:
Show HN: Ribbon Architect is available as a free iOS app and in the browser. Scan or measure a gift, browse pattern suggestions made for its exact proportions, or construct your own designs. Then step-by-step instructions show you how to lay the ribbon on your gift. Gifts are modeled as convex polyhedra, so many non-cuboid gift shapes, such as prisms, work too and have their own interesting ribbon patterns. A ribbon (without twists) that is pulled tight follows a locally shortest path, a geodesic. This is a path on the surface of the gift that runs straight on faces and folds correctly over edges and loops back on itself. As you'll see in the app, geodesics can be much more interesting than the axis-aligned loops that people usually tie when wrapping a gift. Click "Browse geodesics" on the first screen of the app, to get a glimpse of the endless variety of geodesics. (It currently stops after 5'000 or earlier depending on available memory. In theory, a box has infinitely many distinct geodesics.) For further variety, you can combine these building blocks by inserting twists: When twisted, two strands of ribbon that follow sections of geodesics that cross, turn over and follow the other geodesic. This can join two geodesics into a single ribbon. Click any crossing to insert a twist (after selecting a pattern or after drawing ribbons in "draw your own" mode). Or follow the tutorial (the ? icon in the upper right corner). This is the first version. The browser version hasn't been tested on many browsers and devices. Please let me know if you run into any issues.
Website metadata: Plan gift ribbons on a box or any convex shape: ribbons that stay in place without slipping, twisted where they cross.

items.title: Show HN: We replaced our time tracking SaaS with a Git repository
items.description:
Show HN: TL;DR: - Free and open source, no seat limits. - Some of its features require plans that cost a team of 10 around $1,000/year on Clockify or $2,000/year on Toggl Track. - No backend. Your time entries live in your private GitHub repo. - Track any URL. - Works offline, syncs in the background and keeps changes in Git history. - Team reports, CSV exports, historical hourly rates, multiple currencies and PDF invoices, all in the browser. Hi HN. I'm Sergey, one of the developers behind Manticore Search. We'd been using Clockify for years until they decided to limit their free plan to five users recently. We started looking around. Being an open-source company, we weren't particularly excited about paying another monthly fee per employee. But we didn't want to self-host a server and a database for what is essentially a stopwatch either. Then we thought: we already use GitHub for most of our work (dev, PM, CRM, CMS). Why not use it for time tracking too? So we built Clockoli. Our whole team (Manticore Search) switched to it about a month ago, and so far it's been working well for us. Each team member writes to their own branch. Even if we abandon Clockoli tomorrow, your synced data isn't going anywhere. Just git clone the repo and do whatever you want with it: look through the history, write your own scripts, let an AI agent analyze the data or even build your own tools around it. There are downsides, of course. You depend on GitHub. Anyone with read access to the repo can see the team's time entries, so if you need to keep some of them private from your teammates, this might not be for you. Hourly rates, though, are stored in your browser and never committed to the repo. It works for us, but I'm wondering if it would work for other teams too. Would you use something like this? If not, what would stop you?
Website metadata: The Git-native time tracker for teams. Free forever, open-source, serverless. Your GitHub repo is your database. No subscriptions, no seat limits, no vendor lock-in. - Clockoli/clockoli

items.title: Show HN: Rchive – Every drive I've owned since the 90s, searchable in one window
items.description:
Show HN: RCHIVE is a cross-platform desktop app for cataloging, searching and reorganizing files on your computers and drives. Like, all of 'em: internal, external, network shares, USB sticks, loose SD cards, weird CD-R's, DVDs, floppy disks, Zip disks, and everything in between. I built this thing because my digital archives are an embarrassment! 30 years of getting a new hard drive whenever capacity quadrupled and dragging the old one to it into a folder titled "BACKUP - TO SORT" will do that to you lol, especially when you know deep down that "sorting" will never happen. To try to deal with that growing mess on a daily basis, I've tried a patchwork of all of our favorites in the past -- Everything, grep, custom scripts, you name it. And don't get me started on built-in OS defaults like Windows Explorer, Finder, Spotlight. I figured it was time to make something better-suited to my tastes, and 4200 commits later here we are! RCHIVE scans as many different sources as you throw at it, gives you unified deep search across the entire catalog (with drives connected or disconnected), allows you to virtually organize and clean up giant archives of digital stuff by applying recipes and transformations, resiliently copies or moves files when you're ready to actually restructure on disk, or just lets you quickly pop in to find something or browse everything with previews, metadata, etc. It works on Windows, Mac or Linux, works offline, has zero telemetry, deletes nothing, and is fully deterministic in operation. So, no wacky AI integrations for decision making or classification, everything is predictable and repeatable, you can even run portable versions off of a USB drive if you don't want to install it. I've been using it all day every day for a year and am just stoked to have it out there, get some users, get some feedback (good or bad), and see what people think. There's a free trial, no email address or anything needed. The website is also full of videos, features, comparisons, all that stuff, as well as a ncdu -like companion app for figuring out where the hell all your disk space went. Anyways, check it out! Should come in handy if you're ever in Grand Central trying to find a garbage file left on some dude's Gibson. https://www.rchive.computer

items.title: Show HN: Genesis Map – Visualize your agent's changes. See where they can break
items.description:
Show HN: When agent ships code faster and faster, human review is no longer possible. Which brings 2 problems, at least for me: 1. I need to understand what my agent changes as quickly and easily as possible, cuz I don't wanna lose track of the current status of my product, or be the main bottleneck in shipping code. 2. I don't trust what my agent tells me. Many times, I've been suffered from agent telling me "all is well", then say "you are right, sorry, I missed..." after code failed on production. To mitigate those problems, I made Genesis, a skill for coding agent to generate a beautiful flow chart to understand all the business flows, flag all risk changes and untested code between commits. It worked very well on me, so I benchmarked it against vanilla Claude code and Codex: Vanilla → With Genesis 1. Test gaps caught: Claude Code 8% → 38% · Codex 4% → 23% 2. False alarms per review: Claude Code 2.1 → 0.7 · Codex 1.4 → 0.5 3. Real risks found per review: Claude Code 2.9 → 2.8 · Codex 2.4 → 2.4
Website metadata: Turn your codebase into a business flow map and see which of your coding agent's changes are untested or risky. A local CLI and skill for Claude Code, Codex and other agents, for Python, TypeScript and most common languages. - GenesisAgentInfra/genesis

items.title: Show HN: Synth Patch Hero
items.description: Show HN: I wanted to be more deliberate and systematic in how I approach working on synth patches. With the help of our friend Claude, I put together a game that runs through exercises that builds that muscle in a fun and approachable way where you learn as you build patches on a modular rack. I do not have a Eurorack, nor a strong desire to own one (yet); but I do have a bit of other physical gear. I wanted to see if the lessons would translate to boxes, where sound is also better than the browser. So I have started adding groove box specific enhanced lessons (so far just a couple for the Digitone II, but they worked so far). Also: - You can set up MIDI in settings and play your patch in the browser with a MIDI keyboard (Chrome worked, but Safari didn't when I tried). - The Help in the exercises can unblock you when you get stuck and teach you as it helps. - You can pick a groove box in settings under 'my gear' to get some device-specific lessons.

items.title: Show HN: A narrated map tour of the events leading up to the Texas Revolution
items.description:
Show HN: I put together a narrated map of the Texas Revolution. You can listen to a 20-minute audio guided version or just scroll through the events: I thought the chronological and location based timeline made it easier to follow and learn as well. I was inspired by Mapbox’s “storytelling” template on GitHub and built my own version with MapLibre fork of Mapbox GL (with free satellite imagery and terrain tiles from USGS) and lots of help from Claude. There are lots of parameters that were built in, like the rotation and transition speed. Essentially themed it and added source links to the cards. The information was sourced from Handbook of Texas by THC. The voice is AI generated using Elevenlabs v4. That github project https://github.com/mapbox/storytelling has some cool use-case examples that have been published as web features by a few publications. There is so much more you can do with this, like hooking it to live data. The template is a great place to start! Narrations by Elevenlabs TTS. Working on this new one around Houston Oil industry as well. https://whistlestop.guide/features/houston-oil
Website metadata: Fifteen years, told in 21 places. In 1821 Texas was a remote province of a newly independent Mexico, shared uneasily by Tejanos, Comanche and American colonists.
